claims.text: The equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr substrate is in the cast state.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
HfNbTaTiZr has inadequate oxidation resistance for high-temperature use in air.
An anti-oxidation coating is required for high-temperature application of this alloy system in air.
A thin, dense aluminide coating can be deposited on as-cast HfNbTaTiZr by pack cementation or an equivalent treatment.
The aluminide coating will form a continuous, adherent Al2O3 layer during high-temperature exposure.
The alumina layer will act as an effective oxygen-diffusion barrier at the coating–substrate interface.
Preventing oxygen from reaching the substrate will mitigate oxidation-driven embrittlement.
A stable Al2O3 scale hinders further oxidation.
The coating and alumina scale will preserve the substrate microstructure and mechanical integrity.
Coated samples will have significantly lower oxygen uptake, weight gain, or oxide-scale thickness than uncoated samples after exposure.
Coated samples will retain their yield strength and ductility at 1000 °C relative to uncoated samples.
Untreated HfNbTaTiZr undergoes rapid oxidation and mechanical degradation during high-temperature exposure in air.
The proposed test exposure is 1000 °C in air for approximately 100 hours.
The proposed mechanical-loading boundary is tensile testing at strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1 at room temperature and 1000 °C.
Coating adhesion during thermal cycling may limit performance.
The coating process may alter local substrate microstructural features.

contradictions.description: The conditions and boundary imply high-temperature exposure under tensile loading at specified strain rates, whereas the experiment exposes specimens for 100 hours without stated loading and performs tensile tests only afterward.

The hypothesis requires both improved oxidation resistance and no sacrifice of mechanical performance, but the falsification rule uses a conjunction: it requires both failure to reduce oxidation and failure to maintain mechanics. A coating that improves oxidation resistance but severely degrades mechanics would therefore not be declared falsifying under the stated rule.
